strengths: Identifies and quantifies a practically important gap: foundation flow-matching (FM) priors underperform domain-specific and even untrained priors for inverse problems (Table 1, Fig. 2), motivating the need for better use of foundation priors.

Proposes a simple and empirically effective plug-in framework: a learnable time-dependent warm-start (Eq. 3.5) and a sharp shell constraint on the source latent (Eq. 3.8) with closed-form projection (Eq. 3.9).
Extends the idea to a few-shot scientific-imaging setting by optimizing simplex weights over available instances (Eq. 3.10), which is a novel and relevant formulation for domains with limited data.

Provides systematic experiments across multiple datasets (DIV2K, RealSR, AFHQ), tasks (super-resolution, inpainting, Gaussian/motion deblurring), and scientific IPs (LIS, MRI), plus an ablation showing that warm-start gives most of the gain and the shell constraint refines it (Table 6).
Appendix gives detailed hyperparameters for most competing methods (Section A.1), which partially aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central claim of 'saving' foundation FM priors is overclaimed: the method is only applicable when the measurement is close to the object (simple-distortion setting) or when few-shot instances close to the object are available. For general inverse problems, the paper provides no solution, and in scientific IPs the method remains far behind domain-specific priors (e.g., LIS PSNR 31.83 vs. Red-diff 36.55; MRI PSNR 23.26 vs. 28.71 in Table 5).

Theoretical grounding is weak. The shell constraint relies on exact Gaussianity of the latent source distribution (Theorem 3.1), but foundation FM models such as Stable Diffusion 3 use VAE latents that are not necessarily standard Gaussian. The paper only performs scalar mean-variance calibration (Eq. 3.6) and does not validate covariance or full Gaussianity. The projection is heuristic with no convergence analysis.

The warm-start approximation error α_t ε is not controlled or bounded; the method assumes that making t learnable suffices to trade off using y versus introducing bias. This is hand-wavy and lacks formal justification or failure analysis.

Experimental evidence is mixed on perceptual quality: FMPlug is often worse than D-Flow on no-reference metrics such as CLIPIQA and MUSIQ (e.g., Gaussian deblur on AFHQ: FMPlug CLIP 0.21 vs. D-Flow 0.34), yet the paper emphasizes stronger visual quality without analyzing this trade-off.

No dedicated limitations section, broader-impact discussion, or research-ethics treatment, despite experiments on medical MRI data. Issues such as privacy, clinical risk, and hallucination from foundation priors are not discussed.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code release or model checkpoints; data splits, random seeds, and few-shot instance selection are not fully specified. The protocol for the D-Flow few-shot comparison is also not described in enough detail.

Novelty is incremental. The warm-start strategy is closely related to D-Flow's initialization (Eq. 2.4), and shell/spherical Gaussian constraints have appeared in prior diffusion work (e.g., Yang et al., 2024). The main new ingredients are learnable t and few-shot simplex weights, which are relatively straightforward extensions.

Presentation has notation inconsistencies (e.g., ε vs. σ in the shell sets in Eqs. 3.7–3.10; confusing notation in Eq. 3.2) and weak support for surjectivity claims (Table 2 reports only PSNR and LPIPS on 1000 images and is not a proof). No error bars or statistical significance tests are reported.

strengths: Identifies and systematically documents an important performance gap: foundation flow-matching priors underperform domain-specific and even untrained priors for inverse problems.

Proposes a simple yet effective plug-in framework (FMPlug) that combines a time-dependent warm-start strategy with a sharp Gaussianity regularization, yielding substantial improvements over the state-of-the-art plug-in baseline D-Flow.
Provides a theoretical insight using concentration of measure to explain why the initialization strategy in D-Flow is problematic, which motivates the proposed warm-start.

Conducts extensive experiments across multiple image restoration tasks (super-resolution, inpainting, Gaussian/motion deblurring) on three datasets, showing consistent gains over D-Flow and competitive performance with the untrained DIP baseline.
Extends the method to few-shot scientific inverse problems (linear inverse scattering, compressed sensing MRI), demonstrating significant improvements over DIP and D-Flow in those settings.
Includes an ablation study that dissects the contributions of warm-start and Gaussianity regularization, showing that warm-start provides the majority of the performance gain.
Reproducibility is generally good: uses publicly available datasets, pretrained foundation models (Stable Diffusion V3), and provides detailed hyperparameter settings in the appendix.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the warm-start strategy resembles existing noise-scheduling/early-stopping ideas in diffusion/flow models, and the shell constraint on latent variables is a known technique; the combination is incremental.

Overclaimed results: the paper states FMPlug is the 'overall winner by all metrics but CLIPIQA and MUSIQ,' but this is not true for all tasks (e.g., in AFHQ inpainting, DIP achieves higher PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS).

The performance gap to domain-specific priors remains large, especially in scientific inverse problems (e.g., LIS: FMPlug 31.83 vs. Red-diff 36.55 PSNR; MRI: 23.26 vs. 28.71 PSNR), so the practical impact of 'saving' foundation priors is limited.
No dedicated limitations section; the paper does not adequately discuss failure cases, computational cost, or the conditions under which the method may not work well.

The sharp Gaussianity regularization yields only marginal improvements over warm-start alone (ablation: +0.2 dB PSNR), suggesting the main contribution is the warm-start rather than the combined framework.
The comparison with the untrained DIP baseline is mixed: FMPlug does not consistently outperform DIP across all tasks and metrics, yet the paper sometimes implies clear superiority.
Presentation issues: inconsistent method naming in tables (e.g., 'FMPug' vs. 'FMPlug'), messy reference formatting, and minor typos reduce clarity.
The few-shot extension is relatively simple (optimizing convex combination weights over a simplex) and its effectiveness is demonstrated only on two scientific inverse problems.

strengths: Addresses an important and clearly-articulated problem: foundation FM priors (SD3, Flux) underperform even untrained priors for inverse problems. The gap is documented with systematic evidence in Table 1 and Fig. 2 across kernel sizes, which is a valuable observation for the community.

The method is well-motivated by theory. The concentration-of-measure argument that virtually all FM training inputs lie in a thin shell S around S^{d-1}(0,sqrt(d)), so that G_theta is effectively only defined on S, gives a principled explanation for why D-Flow's initialization (Eq. 2.4) lands in S^c and behaves unpredictably. This is a genuinely insightful diagnosis.

Empirical gains are consistent and substantial. FMPlug improves over D-Flow (its main plug-in competitor) on nearly all pixel/structural metrics across 3 datasets and 4 tasks (Table 3), and notably narrows the gap to domain-specific priors in Table 4 (e.g., FMPlug(FD) 29.00 PSNR vs D-Flow(DS) 28.41 on Gaussian blur).

The ablation (Table 6) cleanly isolates the two components: warm-start drives most of the gain, and the sharp Gaussian regularization adds a further consistent improvement, especially in perceptual/CLIPIQA terms.

The few-shot extension (Section 3.3) is a practically relevant contribution for scientific imaging; the simplex/softmax reparameterization for automatic instance selection is a sensible design, and results in Table 5 show large margins over D-Flow and DIP on LIS and MRI.
Reproducibility is reasonably supported: backbone (SD3 Medium), NFE, solvers, learning rates, and dataset/task settings are specified in Section A.1.
weaknesses: Some central claims are overstated. The text states FMPlug is 'the overall winner by all metrics but CLIPIQA and MUSIQ, beating the untrained DIP,' but DIP actually wins PSNR/SSIM on 70% inpainting across AFHQ (33.32 vs 32.81), DIV2K (28.49 vs 28.95 - close), and RealSR (30.88 vs 31.79). More importantly, FMPlug's no-reference perceptual quality (CLIPIQA/MUSIQ) is frequently far below D-Flow (e.g., SR on AFHQ: 0.20 vs 0.31), suggesting the method trades perceptual naturalness for pixel fidelity. This tension deserves explicit discussion rather than being downplayed.

The gap to domain-specific priors is only partially closed. On scientific IPs (Table 5), FMPlug (31.83/0.97 LIS) still trails the domain-specific Red-diff (36.55/0.98) by a wide margin, and the abstract/claims of 'closing the gap' are stronger than what the scientific-IP evidence supports.

There is no dedicated limitations section. The surjectivity assumption on G_theta, which is foundational to the plug-in formulation, is only checked empirically via a single image-regression table (Table 2) and not probed across domains or failure modes; the few-shot assumption that provided instances are close to x is likewise unexamined for robustness.

Comparison fairness is not fully established. FMPlug uses NFE=3 while FlowDPS/FlowChef use NFE=28, and D-Flow uses LBFGS with a different optimizer; the different optimization budgets and solvers make it difficult to attribute gains purely to the proposed components rather than to optimization tuning.

Novelty of the individual ingredients is moderate and partly acknowledged: warm-starting from the measurement is common in diffusion/FM inverse problems, and the spherical/shell constraint is related to prior work (Yang et al., 2024). The main novelty is the combination and the CoM-based justification, which is reasonable but incremental.

The mean-variance calibration requires drawing 4000 unconditional samples and fitting an auxiliary network; the overhead and its sensitivity to the number of samples are not reported, and the benefit is admittedly minor at low noise (Table 7).

strengths: Clearly documents a real and underexplored problem: foundation FM priors underperform domain-specific and untrained priors for inverse problems (Table 1, Figs. 2-3), providing a useful empirical baseline and motivation.

Proposes a simple, practical plug-in framework: a learnable warm-start time t in α_t y + β_t z and a sharp Gaussian shell constraint with a closed-form projection. The method is easy to implement on top of existing foundation FM priors and is motivated by concentration-of-measure intuition.

Extends the framework to few-shot scientific inverse problems by optimizing simplex weights over available instances; demonstrates data efficiency (Table 18) and shows learned weights correlate with ground-truth instance-to-target distances (Spearman -0.71, Pearson -0.79).

Broad evaluation across simple-distortion tasks (super-resolution, inpainting, Gaussian/motion deblurring) and three scientific IPs (LIS, MRI, BKH), with ablations on warm-start time, shell thickness, NFE, runtime, and initialization robustness. FMPlug beats D-Flow and often DIP, and approaches domain-specific Red-Diff on LIS/BKH.
Ablations support the design: learned t* decreases with blur severity (Table 6), warm-start provides most of the gain, and the method is robust to low NFE and random initialization.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the warm-start extends D-Flow's fixed initialization by making t learnable; the shell constraint is a minor variation on existing spherical Gaussian constraints; and the few-shot convex combination is straightforward. Theoretical justification is informal, and the concentration-of-measure argument at t=0 does not rigorously justify the distribution of intermediate-time inputs α_t y + β_t z.

Evaluation uses only Stable Diffusion V3 as the foundation FM backbone; claims about 'foundation FM models' generally are not established across other foundation models (e.g., FLUX). Missing comparisons to recent foundation-prior inverse-problem methods such as DMPlug or other diffusion/flow plug-in baselines.

Overclaims: the statement that FMPlug is the 'overall winner across all metrics except CLIPIQA' is contradicted by AFHQ inpainting, where DIP wins PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS. 'Closing the gap' is only partial—Table 16 shows domain-specific methods still better on several metrics. No statistical significance testing is provided for small gains.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the number of iterations N, optimizer schedule, explicit α_t/β_t schedules for SD3, and code are not provided; details such as how to encode masked/inpainted y in latent space are missing. Presentation is rough with many typos and notation errors ('FMPug', Eq. 3.7 missing ε, garbled Algorithm 1 projection set, Eq. 3.11 missing the shell constraint).

The few-shot assumption that the target is well approximated by a linear combination of few-shot instances is strong and is violated in MRI (acknowledged). There is no protocol for selecting/guaranteeing representative few-shot samples, and potential overlap or leakage between guidance and evaluation is not discussed.

The sharp Gaussian regularization yields only marginal gains (e.g., 26.05→26.26 PSNR in the ablation); most improvement comes from warm-start. The paper does not explore nonlinear simple-distortion inverse problems, and failure modes/limitations are not systematically analyzed.

strengths: Addresses a real and practically relevant problem: the paper systematically documents (Sec. 2.3, Tab. 1, Figs. 2-3) that foundation FM priors underperform domain-specific and even untrained (DIP) priors on inverse problems, which is a useful empirical observation for the community.

The proposed FMPlug is simple, conceptually clean, and appears to deliver consistent empirical gains over D-Flow and DIP across three datasets (AFHQ, DIV2K, RealSR) and four linear tasks, with the few-shot extension giving strong results on scientific IPs (LIS, BKH).

The few-shot instance-guided extension for scientific IPs (Eq. 3.11) is a genuinely novel and potentially impactful application, and the correlation analysis between learned weights and instance-target distance (Spearman -0.71) is a nice validation.

The ablations are informative: they isolate the contribution of warm-start vs. shell regularization (Tab. 5), show learned t* behaves as predicted with degradation level (Tab. 6), and test sensitivity to epsilon, NFE, and random initialization (Tabs. 7, 8, 17, 18).
Reproducibility details (backbone SD3, NFE, solvers, learning rates, optimizers) are largely provided in the appendix, and limitations (e.g., MRI assumption violation) are honestly discussed.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited. The shell/spherical Gaussianity constraint is explicitly acknowledged as pre-existing (Yang et al., 2024), and the time-dependent warm-start is essentially a learnable 'partial-noise' initialization that is well known in the diffusion literature. The ablation shows the regularization contributes only ~0.2 PSNR (Tab. 5), so most of the gain rests on the warm-start alone.

The central empirical claim (beating D-Flow) is partly circular: the paper diagnoses D-Flow's initialization as the failure mode and then fixes exactly that initialization. Fairness of tuning is also unclear, since baselines and the proposed method use different optimizers (LBFGS vs. AdamW) and different regularization settings.

The framing of the 'foundation << domain-specific' gap as a surprising/first-time discovery is overstated: the domain-specific model is trained on the exact test domain (AFHQ-Cat), so its advantage is largely expected, and the paper's own Tab. 16 shows FMPlug(FD) can even exceed DS methods on PSNR, which sits uneasily with the narrative.

FMPlug consistently underperforms on CLIPIQA (no-reference perceptual quality) across essentially all tasks (e.g., 4x SR AFHQ: 0.20 vs. 0.31/0.33 for D-Flow/DIP). The paper dismisses this as unreliable metric behavior rather than investigating whether the method produces over-smoothed outputs that favor distortion metrics.

Theoretical motivation is heuristic: the 'shell S' argument that G_theta is effectively trained only on a thin shell ignores that intermediate-time marginals p_t(z_t) differ across t, and the surjectivity claim is supported only by a weak image-regression experiment (Tab. 2, small PSNR gap).

On scientific IPs the comparison set is thin (only DIP and D-Flow); interleaving methods and other plug-in baselines are not evaluated, and the reported ~5 dB PSNR jump over D-Flow on BKH is large enough to warrant more scrutiny.

Presentation has numerous issues: typos ('obsoleses', 'vise versa'), garbled algorithm notation ('FMPug', 'P_{S_t^{d-1}(0,sqrt(Z))}', 's.t. z in Sd-1(0,sqrt(d))'), and poorly rendered figures, which hinder readability and reproducibility.

strengths: Identifies and quantifies an important performance gap: foundation FM priors (e.g., D-Flow (FD), FlowDPS (FD)) lag behind domain-specific FM and even untrained DIP on Gaussian deblurring (Tab. 1, Figs. 2-3), motivating the need for prior strengthening.

Proposes a simple yet effective plug-in framework, FMPlug, with a time-dependent warm-start that leverages the training-time flow distribution and a sharp Gaussian shell constraint; both are motivated by concentration-of-measure (Thm. 3.1) and address specific deficiencies in D-Flow's initialization and chi-square NLL regularization.

Extensive empirical validation on simple-distortion IPs across three datasets and four tasks shows consistent improvements over D-Flow and DIP on primary reference-based metrics (Tab. 3, Tabs. 10-15), with ablations confirming the contribution of warm-start and regularization (Tab. 5).

Extends the framework to few-shot scientific IPs (LIS, MRI, BKH), demonstrating gains over DIP and D-Flow and approaching domain-specific Red-Diff on LIS/BKH (Tab. 4); the learned instance weights correlate strongly with true similarity (Spearman -0.71, Pearson -0.79), supporting the instance-guided design.

Reproducibility is well-supported: Algorithms 1 and 2, detailed hyperparameters (Sec. A.3), runtime/memory analysis (Tab. 9), and robustness checks (Tabs. 6-8, 17) are provided; datasets and foundation models are public.
The paper is clearly written and organized, and it honestly discusses limitations (e.g., MRI assumption violation, no-reference metric caveats).
weaknesses: Theoretical justification is heuristic rather than rigorous. The critique of D-Flow's initialization assumes a specific norm/shift regime and does not formally prove that the proposed warm-start input distribution matches the training distribution for all t; surjectivity of G_theta is only empirically checked on 1000 DIV2K images (Tab. 2).

The sharp Gaussian regularization provides only a small gain in ablation (Tab. 5: 26.05 to 26.26 PSNR over warm-start only) and is insensitive to epsilon in the tested range (Tab. 7), raising questions about its practical necessity and the strength of the theoretical motivation.

The few-shot scientific evaluation is limited: only three tasks, and MRI shows a large gap to domain-specific Red-Diff (PSNR 23.60 vs 28.71). The key assumption that provided instances contain a close neighbor is violated for MRI, and the method offers no robust fallback beyond weight correlation.

Some claims are overstated. For example, FMPlug is not the best on all reference metrics: on RealSR 4x SR, DIP achieves higher PSNR (26.81 vs 26.66, Tab. 3), and FMPlug consistently underperforms on CLIPIQA/MUSIQ, which are dismissed as secondary despite being widely used.

Reproducibility details are incomplete: the exact alpha_t, beta_t schedule for SD3 and the text prompt extraction for FlowDPS/FlowChef are not fully specified in the manuscript; code availability is not confirmed.
The comparison is limited to SD3 as the foundation FM; generality to other foundation models (e.g., Flux) and other few-shot adaptation methods is not established.
